newsitem.title: INDIA: India considering changes in provident fund rules.
newsitem.headline: India considering changes in provident fund rules.

text.p: India is considering a proposal to allow employee provident funds to make limited investments in highly secured corporate debt instruments, Finance Ministry officials said on Monday.

"There are proposals from the provident fund commissioner to allow the employee provident fund scheme (EPFS) to make limited investments in AAA-rated corporate debt instruments," said a senior finance ministry official who asked not to be identified.
The corporate debt instruments have to be rated by at least two credit rating agencies, he said.
"The proposal will be examined by the finance ministry and then has to be approved by the cabinet," he added.

Currently, the government mandates that 40 percent of the EPFS be invested in bonds and securities issued by state-owned financial institutions, public sector firms and certificates of deposit (CDs) of state-owned banks.
The official said another 25 percent has to be invested in central government securities and 15 percent in guaranteed securities issued by central or state governments.
The remaining 20 percent is required to be invested in the government's special deposit schemes.
The EPFS, which is the largest of the country's three state-administered provident fund schemes, had a corpus of 274.83 billion rupees ($7.7 billion) as of November 1996, officials said.
The employee deposit linked insurance scheme had a corpus of 15.32 billion rupees ($428 million) and the employee pension scheme a corpus of 3.41 billion rupees ($95.2 million).

The official said 244.37 billion rupees ($6.8 billion) of the EPFS corpus was invested in special deposit schemes (SDS) and the rest in central government securities, state government securities and loans, and public sector financial institutions.

About 30 billion rupees ($838 million) are annually added to the SDS corpus by way of interest accruals, of which 40 percent or 12 billion ($335 million) is required to be reinvested in bonds, securities, debt instruments of state-owned financial institutions and CDs of public sector banks.
The provident fund commissioner has sought to add highly rated or highly secured debt instruments of corporates, which were earlier excluded from this list, the official said.
If the proposal is approved by the government then a part of the 12 billion rupees would be available for investment in the capital markets.
The official said the commissioner has stressed that the current yields on provident funds were lower than market rates.
The average yield on total holdings in the EPFS was 11.9 percent in 1995/96 (April-March), the official said. "As far as the special deposit schemes is concerned the yield is 12 percent".
Corporate debt instruments would fetch a high yield of 17 to 18 percent, officials said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
